questions.stem: The following confirm the adequate placement of the Proseal LMA EXCEPT:
options: Cuff pressure of 60 cm H2O
Ability to pass the nasogastric tube through the suction port
Leak pressure of less than 25 cm H2O
Unobstructed inspiratory and expiratory flow
questions.explain: A ProSeal is checked by a good seal (oropharyngeal leak pressure above about 20–25 cmH2O), a gastric tube or gel passing easily down the drain tube, and free, square-wave ventilation. Cuff pressure is not a sign of position: 60 cmH2O is the maximum you should allow (aim for about 40–60), not a test that the mask is in the right place. Note that a leak pressure below 25 cmH2O does not confirm a good seal either.

questions.stem: After the induction of general anaesthesia, you are unable to intubate the patient. You then attempt to ventilate using the face mask but ventilation was also inadequate. O2 saturation has started to drop. What do you do next?
options: Attempt fibreoptic intubation
Attempt to insert laryngeal mask (LMA) for ventilation
Perform tracheostomy
Awaken the patient
questions.explain: Can't intubate, can't oxygenate is following the Difficult Airway Society plan: after failed intubation, move to plan B, a second-generation supraglottic airway (LMA), to oxygenate. If that fails, try face mask once more and wake the patient if you can oxygenate; if you cannot, go to front-of-neck access. Fibreoptic intubation wastes time while desaturating, and a surgical tracheostomy is not the emergency step.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with a history of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is scheduled for an emergency laparotomy. She is awake and alert on arrival to the operating room. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be used as the induction agent in this patient?
options: Etomidate
Ketamine
Propofol
Rocuronium
questions.explain: In a stable, awake patient with asthma and COPD, propofol is the usual choice: it blunts airway reflexes and reduces bronchoconstriction on instrumentation, and in an emergency laparotomy it is given as part of a rapid sequence induction. Ketamine is a bronchodilator and is the better choice if she is actively wheezing or haemodynamically unstable. Etomidate has no bronchodilator effect, and rocuronium is a muscle relaxant, not an induction agent.

questions.stem: A 78-year old patient with a history of facet joint arthropathy, small localized right posterior shoulder skin infection and ischaemic heart disease with severe aortic stenosis (valve area 1 cm2) on clopidogrel stopped for the last 8 days. The anaesthesia is considering the use of neuraxial anaesthesia for the orthopaedic procedure. Which of the following options represents a contraindication to the use of neuraxial anaesthesia in this patient?
options: Facet joint arthropathy
Aortic stenosis
Posterior shoulder skin infection
Clopidogrel stopped for last 8 days
questions.explain: Severe aortic stenosis (valve area 1 cm2 or less) is a relative contraindication to neuraxial anaesthesia: a fixed cardiac output cannot compensate for the sudden fall in afterload from a sympathetic block, risking hypotension and coronary ischaemia. Infection is a contraindication only at the puncture site, not on the shoulder. Clopidogrel needs to be stopped for 7 days, so 8 days is enough. Facet arthropathy may make the block technically harder but is not a contraindication.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman is scheduled for spine surgery which requires neuromonitoring. 2 vials of 1mg Remifentanil have been made up to a total volume of 40mls with saline. What is the concentration per ml?
options: 20mcg
25mcg
40mcg
50mcg
questions.explain: Two 1 mg vials give 2 mg = 2000 mcg. Made up to 40 ml in total, that is 2000 / 40 = 50 mcg per ml. Always label the syringe with the final concentration.

questions.stem: A trauma patient has sustained severe injuries resulting in massive haemorrhage and haemodynamic instability. The anaesthesia team activates the massive transfusion protocol (MTP) cycle 1. Which of these is a component of MTP 1?
options: 1 U Cryoprecipitate
200ml Fresh frozen plasma
4 U PCT
2 CSP
questions.explain: The first massive transfusion pack is based on red cells: 4 units of packed red cells (written "PCT" in our protocol), with plasma, so that blood products are given in a balanced ratio. Cryoprecipitate usually comes in a later pack or when fibrinogen is low. Check the hospital's current MTP for the exact contents of each pack.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Too small a NIBP cuff results in falsely high BP readings.
Intra-arterial line monitoring is based on the principle of oscillometry
3 lead ECG allows for monitoring of inferior lead, aVF.
Pulse oximetry functions well in the presence of venous pulsations.
questions.explain: A cuff that is too small (the bladder should be about 40% of the arm circumference) needs more pressure to occlude the artery, so it over-reads; a cuff that is too big under-reads. Arterial lines use a pressure transducer, not oscillometry (oscillometry is how the NIBP cuff works). A 3-lead ECG usually shows leads I, II or III. Venous pulsations (for example with tricuspid regurgitation or a probe that is too tight) make pulse oximetry unreliable.

questions.stem: The ACC/AHA guidelines outline the evaluation of patients with active cardiac conditions coming for non-cardiac surgery. Which of the following group of patients do not require further workup for their cardiac conditions prior to surgery?
options: Compensated heart failure with history of atrial fibrillation
Decompensated heart failure and history of MI
3rd degree heart block with concurrent severe aortic stenosis
Unstable coronary syndrome and 1st degree AV block
questions.explain: The ACC/AHA "active cardiac conditions" that need evaluation and treatment before non-cardiac surgery are unstable coronary syndromes, decompensated heart failure, significant arrhythmias (such as high-grade AV block) and severe valve disease. Compensated heart failure with rate-controlled atrial fibrillation is not an active condition, so it does not need further work-up before surgery. Each of the other options includes at least one active condition.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of knee pain is scheduled for a total knee replacement. She is currently taking oral morphine 10mg every 8 hours for pain control. What is the equivalent intravenous morphine 24-hour requirement for this patient?
options: 10mg
20mg
30mg
40mg
questions.explain: Oral morphine 10 mg every 8 hours is 30 mg a day. Intravenous morphine is about three times as potent as oral (oral to IV ratio about 3:1), so 30 / 3 = 10 mg IV in 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman weighing 60kg is scheduled for a hip replacement surgery. She will be given a fascia iliaca block with 40mls ropivacaine. What is the maximum toxic dose of ropivacaine that should not be exceeded in this patient?
options: 60mg
120mg
180mg
240mg
questions.explain: The maximum safe dose of ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg. For 60 kg that is 3 x 60 = 180 mg. With 40 ml for a fascia iliaca block, the concentration must be 0.45% or less (for example 0.375% x 40 ml = 150 mg) to stay under the limit.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, well-controlled asthma, and ischaemic heart disease s/p PCI 2 years ago is classified as ASA
questions.explain: ASA 3 means severe systemic disease. Coronary artery disease with a stent more than 3 months ago is one of the ASA's own ASA 3 examples. Treated hypertension, diabetes and well-controlled asthma would each be ASA 2 alone, but the ischaemic heart disease makes this patient ASA 3.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman weighing 40kg is scheduled for a removal of lump in her arm. She will be given IV paracetamol during her anaesthetic. The vial is labelled paracetamol 1000mg in 100ml. How much volume of IV paracetamol should be given to her?
options: 100ml
90ml
60ml
40ml
questions.explain: IV paracetamol is 15 mg/kg for patients 50 kg or less: 15 x 40 = 600 mg. At 1000 mg in 100 ml (10 mg/ml), that is 60 ml. Giving the whole 100 ml vial (1 g) is for adults over 50 kg.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient was scheduled for an endoscopy procedure under sedation and monitored anaesthetic care. A 100mcg vial of Fentanyl was drawn up and made up to 10 ml. At the end of the case, 6ml was remaining in the syringe. The AU nurse is tallying the CDs. How much Fentanyl was used during the case?
options: 10mcg
20mcg
40mcg
60mcg
questions.explain: 100 mcg made up to 10 ml is 10 mcg per ml. 6 ml is left, so 4 ml was used: 4 x 10 = 40 mcg. Record the amount given and discard the rest with a witness, as for every controlled drug.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient weighing 70kg is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. Intubation with an ETT is planned. What is the most likely dose of IV atracurium given to this patient at induction?
options: 20mg
30mg
35mg
40mg
questions.explain: The intubating dose of atracurium is 0.5 mg/kg: 0.5 x 70 = 35 mg. Onset is about 2–3 minutes and it lasts about 30–40 minutes.

questions.stem: You are reviewing a 50 year old male for elective spine surgery in PEC. He has some recent URTI 3 weeks ago. His ECG is shown below. What is your main differential diagnosis?
options: Hyperkalaemia
Myocardial ischaemia
Brugada pattern
Right bundle branch block
questions.explain: Brugada pattern: in V1 and V2 the ST segment rises 2 mm or more from the end of the QRS and slopes down in a "coved" shape into an inverted T wave (type 1, the diagnostic pattern). It can look like right bundle branch block, but RBBB has an rSR' without the coved ST elevation. It matters before anaesthesia because fever, some drugs (for example sodium channel blockers and high-dose propofol) and electrolyte changes can trigger ventricular arrhythmias, so the patient needs a cardiology review before elective surgery. ECG: PeaBrainC, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

questions.stem: Management of laryngospasm includes all the following EXCEPT
options: CPAP
Suxamethonium 100mg IV
Propofol 50mg IV
Increase FiO2
questions.explain: Laryngospasm is treated by removing the stimulus, 100% oxygen, CPAP with a tight mask, jaw thrust, and deepening anaesthesia with propofol (about 0.5–1 mg/kg). If it persists, a small dose of suxamethonium (about 0.1–0.5 mg/kg, for example 10–20 mg) usually breaks it; 1–2 mg/kg (around 100 mg) is the intubating dose, used if you need to intubate. The key takes the 100 mg dose as the exception.

questions.stem: You have been asked by the consultant anaesthetist to give adrenaline in a crisis situation. She passes you a syringe labelled 'adrenaline 1:10,000'. You gave 1 ml from this syringe. How much of adrenaline was given to the patient?
options: 1 mg
100 mcg
10 mcg
1 mcg
questions.explain: 1:10,000 means 1 g in 10,000 ml = 0.1 mg per ml. So 1 ml contains 0.1 mg = 100 mcg. (1:1,000 is 1 mg per ml, the strength used for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis.)

questions.stem:
A 65 year old patient with history of diverticulitis for exploratory laparotomy has been listed as a P2. His ABG is below. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s acid-base disturbance?
pH 7.30  PaCO2 28  HCO3 16  Lactate 4
options: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
questions.explain: pH 7.30 is an acidaemia, and a low bicarbonate (16) means the primary problem is a metabolic acidosis, here with a raised lactate (for example sepsis from diverticulitis). The PaCO2 is low, so the lungs are compensating, but the pH is not normal, so it is only partially compensated. By Winter's formula the expected PaCO2 is 1.5 x 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2; 28 is lower than that, suggesting an extra respiratory alkalosis as well.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man undergoing laparoscopic colectomy under general anesthesia begins to desaturate. His SpO2 drops from 99% to 90% over 2 minutes. Capnography is normal. The FiO2 is increased to 1.0. On auscultation, breath sounds are decreased on the left. Airway pressures have increased. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform needle decompression of the right chest
Suction the endotracheal tube and assess for obstruction
Confirm endotracheal tube position and check for right mainstem intubation
Increase tidal volume and respiratory rate
questions.explain: Desaturation with high airway pressures and reduced breath sounds on the left after intubation suggests the tube has slipped into the right main bronchus. It is common in laparoscopic surgery, because the pneumoperitoneum and head-down tilt push the carina up towards the tube tip. Check the tube depth, listen to both sides and pull the tube back. A tension pneumothorax on the left would need left-sided decompression, not right; increasing ventilation does not fix the cause.

questions.stem: During preoperative assessment, a patient’s physical examination reveals that the elderly patient has a full beard, limited mandibular protrusion and a short thyromental distance. Which is the most significant predictor of difficult airway management in this patient during anaesthesia induction?
options: Elderly patient
Full beard
Limited mandibular protrusion
Short thyromental distance
questions.explain: Of these findings, a short thyromental distance (under about 6 cm) is the best single predictor of difficult laryngoscopy, because it means little space to displace the tongue. Limited mandibular protrusion also predicts difficulty, and some would rank it higher. A beard makes mask ventilation harder, and older age is a risk for difficult mask ventilation, but neither predicts difficult intubation as strongly.

questions.stem: A 50-year old patient is scheduled for elective surgery requiring general anaesthesia. As part of the preoperative assessment, you examine the patient’s airway and assess for potential indicators of difficult intubation. The patient presents with a thyromental distance of 5cm, a mouth opening of 2.5cm and limited neck range of motion. Which of the following statements is the most accurate interpretation of these findings?
options: The patient has a high likelihood of easy intubation due to the acceptable thyromental distance of 5cm
The patient is at low risk for difficult intubation since the mouth opening of 2.5cm is acceptable
The patient’s limited neck range of motion is the sole concern for potential difficult intubation
The patient’s thyromental distance, mouth opening and neck movements increase the risk of difficult intubation
questions.explain: A thyromental distance under about 6 cm, a mouth opening under about 3 cm and limited neck movement each predict a difficult laryngoscopy. Together they add up, so this patient is at higher risk and needs a plan for a difficult airway. None of the measurements here is reassuring on its own.

questions.stem: Your consultant tasked you to perform manual inline stabilization for tracheal intubation. Which of the following statements is false?
options: This is a potential difficult airway situation.
This is done to protect from cervical spine injury during intubation.
This can be performed either at the cephalad or caudad position with respect to the patient’s head.
This adequately prevents further cervical spine injuries.
questions.explain: Manual in-line stabilisation reduces neck movement during laryngoscopy but does not abolish it, so it does not guarantee that the cervical spine is protected (the false statement). It makes the view worse, so it is a potential difficult airway. The assistant can hold the head from above (cephalad) or from the side or front of the patient (caudad).

questions.stem: During a surgical procedure, a patient develops fast atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 160 beats per minute. The patient’s blood pressure drops to 70/40. What is the most appropriate immediate step in the intraoperative management?
options: Administer synchronized electrical cardioversion
Administer intravenous amiodarone
Administer intravenous digoxin
Continue monitoring without intervention
questions.explain: Fast atrial fibrillation with hypotension (BP 70/40) is unstable, so the treatment is immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. Amiodarone is for stable patients, or after cardioversion; digoxin is too slow to act in this setting. Doing nothing is not appropriate in a haemodynamically unstable patient.

questions.stem: A patient in the PACU following surgery complains of nausea and begins to vomit. The patient has had no antiemetic prophylaxis and is awake, alert and haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment for the patient’s nausea and vomiting in the PACU?
options: Administer intravenous metoclopramide
Administer intravenous droperidol
Administer intravenous ondansetron
Continue monitoring without intervention
questions.explain: For PONV in a patient who had no prophylaxis, a 5-HT3 antagonist such as ondansetron (4 mg IV) is the first-line rescue. If prophylaxis had been given, rescue should use a drug from a different class. Metoclopramide at the usual 10 mg dose is a weak antiemetic for PONV; droperidol works but carries QT and sedation concerns.

questions.stem: A 45-year old patient is scheduled for an elective surgery requiring general anaesthesia. The patient’s surgery is planned for 8:00 AM. According to fasting guidelines, when should the patient be allowed to have clear liquids prior to surgery?
options: Until 6:00 AM on the day of the surgery
Until 12:00 AM (midnight) on the day of the surgery
Until 10:00 PM the day before surgery
Until 08:00 PM the day before surgery
questions.explain: Current fasting guidelines allow clear fluids up to 2 hours before anaesthesia (and solid food up to 6 hours). For an 08:00 start, clear fluids can be taken until 06:00. Keeping patients nil by mouth from midnight makes them thirsty and dehydrated, with no benefit.

questions.stem: During maintenance of anaesthesia in an orthopaedic surgery, a patient experiences sudden and forceful closure of the vocal cords, leading to laryngospasm. Of the following options below, which is the most common risk factor for the occurrence of laryngospasm during anaesthesia?
options: Insufficient depth of anaesthesia
Chronic smoking
Maintained spontaneous ventilation
Absence of secretions in the airway
questions.explain: Laryngospasm is most often triggered by stimulating the airway (secretions, blood, suction, airway insertion or surgery) while anaesthesia is too light. Children, recent upper respiratory tract infection, smoking and airway surgery also raise the risk. Secretions in the airway increase the risk, so their absence is not a risk factor.

questions.stem: What are the precalculated doses of drugs used in a rapid sequence induction (fentanyl, propofol, suxamethonium, followed by atracurium after induction)?
options: Fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg; propofol 20-30 mg/kg; suxamethonium 1-2 mg/kg; then atracurium 0.5 mg/kg
Fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg; propofol 2-3 mg/kg; suxamethonium 10-20 mg/kg; then atracurium 0.5 mg/kg
Fentanyl 10-20 mcg/kg; propofol 2-3 mg/kg; suxamethonium 1-2 mg/kg; then atracurium 0.5 mg/kg
Fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg; propofol 2-3 mg/kg; suxamethonium 1-2 mg/kg; then atracurium 0.5 mg/kg
questions.explain: Typical RSI doses: fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg, propofol 2–3 mg/kg (less in the elderly or unstable), suxamethonium 1–1.5 mg/kg (up to 2 mg/kg), then atracurium 0.5 mg/kg once suxamethonium wears off. Each wrong option has one dose ten times too high.

questions.stem: Atracurium:
options: Is degraded by ester hydrolysis
Is potentiated by hyperthermia
In high doses acts faster than suxamethonium
Can cause bradycardia
questions.explain: Atracurium is broken down by Hofmann elimination (spontaneous, depending on temperature and pH) and by ester hydrolysis by non-specific plasma esterases, so its action does not depend on the liver or kidneys. Hypothermia slows Hofmann elimination and prolongs it, so hyperthermia does not potentiate it. Even in high doses it is slower in onset than suxamethonium. Its histamine release causes hypotension and tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing surgery suddenly develops wheezing and signs of respiratory distress shortly after induction of anaesthesia. The anaesthesia team suspects aspiration of gastric contents. What is the most common risk factor profile for the occurrence of aspiration during anaesthesia?
options: Young age and obesity
History of smoking and asthma
Recent upper respiratory tract infection
Gastrooesophageal reflux disease with hiatal hernia
questions.explain: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with a hiatus hernia lowers the barrier at the lower oesophageal sphincter, which makes regurgitation and aspiration more likely, especially in emergencies, obesity, pregnancy and when the stomach is full. Smoking, asthma and a recent cold increase airway irritability and bronchospasm, but they are not the main risk factors for aspiration.

questions.stem: Hypotension in the recovery may be due to:
options: Inadequate pain control
Inadequate volume replacement
Hypoglycaemia
Inaccurate transducer placement with the NIBP
questions.explain: The commonest cause of hypotension in recovery is hypovolaemia: inadequate fluid replacement, ongoing bleeding or a vasodilated patient after anaesthesia or a neuraxial block. Pain usually raises the blood pressure, and hypoglycaemia is not a usual cause. A non-invasive cuff has no transducer, so transducer position is a source of error for an arterial line, not for NIBP.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.

What do you do first?
options: Start the induction: 62% will do because your consultant is here.
Turn the oxygen flow up to 15 L/min and keep the same grip.
Fix the seal first: reposition the mask, use two hands, sit him up a little, and keep going until the EtO2 is over 80%, ideally 90% or more.
questions.explain:
Right. A leak lets room air in, so the EtO2 can’t rise. The handbook’s minimum is an EtO2 above 80%; aim for 90% or more, because the oxygen stored in his lungs is what keeps him safe while he isn’t breathing. A beard and a BMI of 31 also warn you that bagging may be hard: worth saying out loud now.

The other choices:
• “Start the induction: 62% will do because your consultant is here.” Your consultant shakes their head: “Let’s get the EtO2 up first.” The handbook’s minimum is above 80%, and you should aim for 90%. Heavier patients and men with beards are exactly the ones who desaturate fast and are hard to bag.
• “Turn the oxygen flow up to 15 L/min and keep the same grip.” More flow doesn’t fix a leak: room air is still sucked in around the mask with every breath. Fix the seal (two hands if needed, a little head-up) and watch the EtO2 climb.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 1

questions.stem:
With two hands and a better seal the bag moves well. After 3 minutes the EtO2 is 91%. Your consultant: “Fentanyl 100 mcg is in. Go ahead with the propofol.”

The case so far: A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.

Which is the best choice?
options: Give propofol 150 mg (about 1.8 mg/kg) steadily over about 30 seconds, talking to him, and watch him go off.
Give propofol 300 mg quickly so he is definitely asleep.
Give rocuronium 50 mg first, then the propofol, so the airway is easier.
questions.explain:
The handbook dose is 1–2 mg/kg; for a fit 85 kg man 150 mg is about right. Give it steadily, not as a slam, and watch: the eyelash reflex going and his breathing slowing tell you it is working.

The other choices:
• “Give propofol 300 mg quickly so he is definitely asleep.” 300 mg is about 3.5 mg/kg, well above the 1–2 mg/kg range, and a fast push drops the blood pressure hard. Your consultant stops you: give a sensible dose and titrate to effect.
• “Give rocuronium 50 mg first, then the propofol, so the airway is easier.” Never paralyse an awake patient: it is terrifying and dangerous. And the department’s order (handbook step 8) is to give the muscle relaxant only after you have shown you can bag. Your consultant stops you.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 2

questions.stem:
He stops responding, the eyelash reflex has gone and he stops breathing. You lift the jaw and squeeze the bag with the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve at 20 cmH2O. The chest hardly rises, the bag feels stiff and the capnograph shows only a tiny bump.

The case so far: A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.

Which is the best choice?
options: Say it out loud: “I’m finding this hard to bag.” Then fix the basics: head tilt, chin lift, a firm jaw thrust and a better mask seal.
Close the APL valve fully and squeeze hard to force gas in.
Reach for the rocuronium: once he is relaxed, bagging will be easier.
Keep trying quietly with one hand; you don’t want to look as if you can’t do it.
questions.explain:
Saying it early is the most useful thing you can do: your consultant can only help with a problem they know about. Then the basics: head position, jaw thrust and a good seal fix most difficult mask ventilation.

The other choices:
• “Close the APL valve fully and squeeze hard to force gas in.” High pressure blows gas into the stomach rather than the lungs. That makes regurgitation and aspiration more likely, and a full stomach makes bagging even harder. Keep the APL valve around 20 cmH2O and fix the airway instead.
• “Reach for the rocuronium: once he is relaxed, bagging will be easier.” Your consultant stops your hand. The handbook rule is the reverse: give the relaxant only after you have shown you can bag (step 8). In experienced hands a relaxant sometimes makes bagging easier, but that is your consultant’s decision after the basics, not yours. Meanwhile the saturation is falling.
• “Keep trying quietly with one hand; you don’t want to look as if you can’t do it.” Everyone finds some patients hard to bag. Struggling in silence spends the oxygen you built up. The department rule: when anything is out of the ordinary, the first step is to call for help.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 3

questions.stem:
With a firm jaw thrust and a better seal the chest moves a little and the capnograph shows small waves, but it is still hard work.

The case so far: A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.

Which is the best choice?
options: Stop and let the propofol wear off so he wakes up.
Ask the AU (anaesthetic unit) nurse for a supraglottic airway straight away.
Put in a nasopharyngeal airway.
Put in an oropharyngeal airway (sized from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw) and switch to two hands on the mask while your consultant squeezes the bag.
questions.explain:
Exactly. The oral airway lifts the tongue off the back of the throat, and two hands give the best seal and jaw thrust.

The other choices:
• “Stop and let the propofol wear off so he wakes up.” Propofol can’t be reversed, and while it wears off he still needs oxygen. Waking up is a plan for a failed airway, but only while you keep oxygenating. Keep ventilating and improve the airway.
• “Ask the AU (anaesthetic unit) nurse for a supraglottic airway straight away.” Your consultant: “Get it ready, but let’s try an oral airway and two hands first.” A supraglottic airway is the right rescue if the basics fail, and having it ready is good thinking.
• “Put in a nasopharyngeal airway.” It helps too, but in a deeply unconscious patient an oral airway is quicker and doesn’t risk a nosebleed. The nasal airway is useful when the jaw is clenched or the patient is lighter.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 4

questions.stem:
With the airway adjunct in and two hands on the mask, the chest rises well, the bag feels soft and the capnograph shows a square trace. Your consultant: “Good. Now what?”

The case so far: A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.

Which is the best choice?
options: Give rocuronium, then stop bagging while it works so the stomach doesn’t fill with gas.
Give rocuronium and intubate straight away.
Give rocuronium 50 mg (about 0.6 mg/kg) and keep bagging for about 3 minutes until it has fully worked, then laryngoscopy.
questions.explain:
The handbook order exactly: show you can bag, then give the relaxant (step 8), and keep bagging while it takes effect, about 3 minutes (step 9).

The other choices:
• “Give rocuronium, then stop bagging while it works so the stomach doesn’t fill with gas.” Gentle bagging at 20 cmH2O through a clear airway sends gas to the lungs, not the stomach. Stopping now wastes the oxygen reserve you have just rebuilt. Keep bagging (step 9).
• “Give rocuronium and intubate straight away.” Rocuronium at 0.6 mg/kg takes 2–3 minutes to give good intubating conditions. Going in early means a cough, moving cords and a poor view. Your consultant asks you to wait and keep bagging.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 5

questions.stem:
Three minutes later you look with the laryngoscope, see the cords and pass a size 8.0 tube. You inflate the cuff. How do you confirm it is in the trachea?

The case so far: A 45-year-old man, 85 kg, BMI 31, ASA 2 (treated hypertension, snores, full beard), for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. The agreed plan: fentanyl, propofol, rocuronium and a tracheal tube. Monitors are on and your consultant stands beside you: “Your induction. I’m right here.” You hold the face mask on with one hand. After a minute the end-tidal oxygen (EtO2) reads only 62%, the reservoir bag barely moves and you can hear a hiss around his beard.
options: The SpO2 is still 99%, so the tube must be in the trachea.
You saw it go through the cords, so it is in.
Look for a sustained square capnography trace over several breaths, both sides of the chest rising, and breath sounds in both armpits (and none over the stomach).
questions.explain:
A sustained trace is the one check you can never skip: no trace, wrong place. Chest rise and listening on both sides (handbook step 11) tell you it isn’t too deep.

The other choices:
• “The SpO2 is still 99%, so the tube must be in the trachea.” After good preoxygenation the saturation can stay high for minutes with the tube in the oesophagus. Saturation is a late sign; the capnograph is the early one.
• “You saw it go through the cords, so it is in.” Even experts are sometimes wrong about what they saw. Confirm every tube with sustained capnography.
questions.source: MO guide case: Your first induction (first-induction), step 6

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.

What do you do first?
options: Check the finger probe first: it is probably a poor signal.
Turn the oxygen to 100%, ask the AU nurse to call your consultant, and look at the capnograph trace and the airway pressure.
Give salbutamol through the circuit: she has asthma.
Turn the sevoflurane up: she may be light.
questions.explain:
Oxygen and help first, then look for the cause. The capnograph and the airway pressure are the fastest clues you have.

The other choices:
• “Check the finger probe first: it is probably a poor signal.” The pleth trace looks good and the number is falling steadily: treat it as real. Look at the probe after you have given oxygen and called.
• “Give salbutamol through the circuit: she has asthma.” You don’t know the cause yet, and treating a guess wastes time. Oxygen and help first, then look for the cause step by step.
• “Turn the sevoflurane up: she may be light.” Nothing here suggests she is light, and a deeper anaesthetic does nothing for a falling saturation. Oxygen, help, then look for the cause.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 1

questions.stem:
Oxygen is at 100% and your consultant is on the way. The capnograph shows a normal square trace with every breath, EtCO2 32 mmHg. Peak airway pressure is 30 cmH2O; it was 18 just after intubation. What does the capnograph tell you?

The case so far: A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.
options: The tube is in the oesophagus: take it out.
The tube is in the airway (a sustained trace rules out the oesophagus). Something else is wrong: work through DOPES.
The trace is normal, so the oximeter must be wrong.
questions.explain:
Right. A sustained square trace means the tube is in the trachea or a bronchus. Now DOPES: Displacement (out, or too deep), Obstruction (kink, secretions, biting), Pneumothorax, Equipment (circuit, oxygen supply, ventilator), Stacking of breaths (and bronchospasm).

The other choices:
• “The tube is in the oesophagus: take it out.” A sustained trace with every breath can’t come from the oesophagus. Taking out a tube that is in the airway turns one problem into two.
• “The trace is normal, so the oximeter must be wrong.” A normal capnograph doesn’t mean normal oxygenation. A tube in one lung gives a good trace while blood flowing past the other lung picks up no oxygen. Think again.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 2

questions.stem:
Your consultant is still a minute away. How do you work through it?

The case so far: A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.
options: Pass a suction catheter down the tube.
Switch to the bag on 100% oxygen to feel the lungs, look at both sides of the chest, listen in both armpits, and read the tube length at the teeth.
Ask for a chest X-ray.
questions.explain:
Hand ventilating lets you feel how stiff the lungs are; looking and listening tells you whether both sides are working; the length at the teeth tells you about displacement. Quick and thorough.

The other choices:
• “Pass a suction catheter down the tube.” Reasonable, since it checks for obstruction: the catheter passes easily and there are no secretions. But hand ventilating, looking and listening would have told you more, faster.
• “Ask for a chest X-ray.” Far too slow while the saturation is falling. Your eyes, your ears and your hand on the bag come first.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 3

questions.stem:
The right side of the chest rises more than the left and breath sounds are quiet on the left. The bag feels a little stiff. The tube is at 25 cm at the teeth.

The case so far: A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.

Which is the best choice?
options: It’s a left pneumothorax: ask for a cannula to decompress the chest.

Tell your consultant as they walk in: “The tube is at 25 cm and air entry is quiet on the left: I think it’s in the right main bronchus.” With their OK, let the cuff down, pull back to 21 cm, reinflate and listen again.
Pull the tube back 10 cm to be sure it’s out of the bronchus.
It’s bronchospasm: give salbutamol.
questions.explain:
Yes. In most women the tube sits about 21 cm at the teeth (about 23 cm in men). Too deep, it slips into the right main bronchus, which is wider and straighter, and the left lung gets no ventilation.

The other choices:
• “It’s a left pneumothorax: ask for a cannula to decompress the chest.” A tension pneumothorax brings falling blood pressure, a rising heart rate and a silent, overinflated side. Here the tube is plainly too deep: fix the simple, likely cause first. Your consultant asks you to look at the tube again.
• “Pull the tube back 10 cm to be sure it’s out of the bronchus.” That puts the cuff at or above the cords. Make small moves, with the cuff down, and listen after each.
• “It’s bronchospasm: give salbutamol.” Bronchospasm wheezes on both sides and slopes the capnograph trace. One quiet side with a deep tube is a tube problem.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 4

questions.stem:
Air entry is now equal, peak pressure 19 cmH2O and SpO2 back to 99%. The tube is retaped at 21 cm and your consultant goes back to the control room. Twenty minutes into surgery, as the surgeon starts dissecting, the peak pressure climbs to 34 cmH2O, you hear wheeze on both sides, and the capnograph upstroke slopes like a shark fin.

The case so far: A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.

Which is the best choice?
options: Give more rocuronium.
100% oxygen, call your consultant, deepen the anaesthetic (sevoflurane opens the airways), give salbutamol into the circuit, and check for anaphylaxis and for a kinked or bitten tube.
Pull the tube back again: it must have slipped in.
Turn up the breathing rate to bring the EtCO2 down.
questions.explain:
This is bronchospasm, probably light anaesthesia meeting surgical stimulation in an asthmatic. A deeper volatile and salbutamol (6–10 puffs through an adaptor into the circuit, repeated) treat it. Always look for anaphylaxis (rash, falling blood pressure) and a mechanical cause too.

The other choices:
• “Give more rocuronium.” Muscle relaxants relax skeletal muscle, not the smooth muscle of the airways. A relaxant helps if she is coughing on the tube, but it doesn’t treat bronchospasm.
• “Pull the tube back again: it must have slipped in.” Wheeze on both sides with a sloping trace is the small airways, not the tube position, and the tube is still at 21 cm. Pulling back now risks extubation.
• “Turn up the breathing rate to bring the EtCO2 down.” In bronchospasm the problem is getting gas out. A faster rate leaves less time to breathe out, so gas is trapped and the pressures climb further.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 5

questions.stem:
After two doses of salbutamol and a deeper anaesthetic the wheeze is easing: peak pressure 26 cmH2O, SpO2 97%. Your consultant asks how you would set the ventilator.

The case so far: A 52-year-old woman, 70 kg, with mild asthma (a salbutamol inhaler she rarely needs), for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. You intubated her with a size 7.0 tube under your consultant’s eye; the AU nurse taped it and you switched to the ventilator. Your consultant has gone to the control room to take a call (“Call me for anything”). Three minutes later the pitch of the oximeter tone starts to drop.

Which is the best choice?
options: Add PEEP of 15 cmH2O to hold the airways open.
A faster rate with smaller breaths.
A slower rate and a longer time to breathe out (I:E ratio 1:3), accepting an EtCO2 a little higher than usual.
questions.explain:
Giving time to breathe out lets the trapped gas escape and brings the pressures down. A slightly higher CO2 does no harm for a while.

The other choices:
• “Add PEEP of 15 cmH2O to hold the airways open.” High PEEP adds to the trapped gas and the pressure in the chest. Keep a modest PEEP and give time to breathe out.
• “A faster rate with smaller breaths.” A faster rate shortens the time to breathe out, which is the opposite of what she needs.
questions.source: MO guide case: SpO2 falling after intubation (desat-intubated), step 6

questions.stem:
A 78-year-old woman, 55 kg, for a cystoscopy and resection of a bladder tumour under GA with a supraglottic airway. She takes amlodipine and losartan and took both this morning. Before induction her BP was 165/85. Because of her age your consultant asked you to draw up phenylephrine and ephedrine. Your consultant induced with fentanyl 50 mcg and propofol 70 mg, the airway went in easily, and she is breathing sevoflurane at 2.5%. Your consultant has stepped next door to help a colleague (“Call me if anything changes”). As she is put into lithotomy the next BP reads 72/40.

What do you do first?
options: Ask the AU nurse to call your consultant now; turn the sevoflurane down; set the BP to cycle every minute and recheck it.
Give phenylephrine 100 mcg first, and call if it doesn’t work.
Wait for the next automatic reading in 5 minutes: cuff readings are often wrong in lithotomy.
Turn the sevoflurane off completely.
questions.explain:
Do both at once: get help coming and start the simple fixes. Too much anaesthetic for an elderly patient is the commonest cause: 2.5% sevoflurane is well over 1 MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) at 78, when 1 MAC is only about 1.6% (about 2% in a 40-year-old).

The other choices:
• “Give phenylephrine 100 mcg first, and call if it doesn’t work.” Treating quickly is good, but the handbook’s first step when anything is out of the ordinary is to call for help. You can do both: ask the nurse to call while you act. And with a heart rate of 56, ephedrine suits her better than phenylephrine.
• “Wait for the next automatic reading in 5 minutes: cuff readings are often wrong in lithotomy.” Assume a low reading is real until you have proved otherwise. Recheck it now, not in 5 minutes.
• “Turn the sevoflurane off completely.” Turning it off risks awareness. Turn it down to about 1 MAC for her age (about 1.5–1.6%) and support the blood pressure. Try again.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after induction (hypotension-induction), step 1

questions.stem:
Help is on the way and the sevoflurane is down at 1.5%. The BP cycles again: 70/42, heart rate 54. The ephedrine and phenylephrine syringes are labelled on your tray.

The case so far: A 78-year-old woman, 55 kg, for a cystoscopy and resection of a bladder tumour under GA with a supraglottic airway. She takes amlodipine and losartan and took both this morning. Before induction her BP was 165/85. Because of her age your consultant asked you to draw up phenylephrine and ephedrine. Your consultant induced with fentanyl 50 mcg and propofol 70 mg, the airway went in easily, and she is breathing sevoflurane at 2.5%. Your consultant has stepped next door to help a colleague (“Call me if anything changes”). As she is put into lithotomy the next BP reads 72/40.

Which is the best choice?
options: Run in a litre of fluid and wait.
Ephedrine 5 mg IV (1 mL of 5 mg/mL), repeated in 2–3 minutes if needed.
Phenylephrine 100 mcg IV (1 mL of 100 mcg/mL).
questions.explain:
With a slow heart rate, ephedrine is a good first choice: it raises both the heart rate and the blood pressure.

The other choices:
• “Run in a litre of fluid and wait.” Fluid helps if she is dry, but it takes minutes to work and a litre is a lot for a 78-year-old heart. The problem here is mostly drug-induced widening of the vessels: give a vasopressor now.
• “Phenylephrine 100 mcg IV (1 mL of 100 mcg/mL).” It will raise the blood pressure, but phenylephrine only squeezes the vessels, and the reflex response can slow the heart further. It is best when the heart rate is normal or fast.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after induction (hypotension-induction), step 2

questions.stem:
Two minutes later the BP is 90/52, heart rate 66. Your consultant walks in: “What’s happening?”

The case so far: A 78-year-old woman, 55 kg, for a cystoscopy and resection of a bladder tumour under GA with a supraglottic airway. She takes amlodipine and losartan and took both this morning. Before induction her BP was 165/85. Because of her age your consultant asked you to draw up phenylephrine and ephedrine. Your consultant induced with fentanyl 50 mcg and propofol 70 mg, the airway went in easily, and she is breathing sevoflurane at 2.5%. Your consultant has stepped next door to help a colleague (“Call me if anything changes”). As she is put into lithotomy the next BP reads 72/40.

Which is the best choice?
options: Start with her history from the pre-op clinic.

“BP fell to 72/40 as she went into lithotomy, about 8 minutes after induction, heart rate 56. I turned the sevoflurane down to 1.5% and gave ephedrine 5 mg; it’s now 90/52. She took losartan and amlodipine this morning.”
“Her BP dropped, but it’s better now.”
questions.explain:
Short, in order, with the numbers and what you have done: your consultant can decide in seconds.

The other choices:
• “Start with her history from the pre-op clinic.” Lead with the problem and the numbers. The history comes after, if asked.
• ““Her BP dropped, but it’s better now.”” Too vague. Your consultant needs the lowest value, for how long, what you gave and what it is now. Try again.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after induction (hypotension-induction), step 3

questions.stem:
Your consultant: “What do you think caused it?”

The case so far: A 78-year-old woman, 55 kg, for a cystoscopy and resection of a bladder tumour under GA with a supraglottic airway. She takes amlodipine and losartan and took both this morning. Before induction her BP was 165/85. Because of her age your consultant asked you to draw up phenylephrine and ephedrine. Your consultant induced with fentanyl 50 mcg and propofol 70 mg, the airway went in easily, and she is breathing sevoflurane at 2.5%. Your consultant has stepped next door to help a colleague (“Call me if anything changes”). As she is put into lithotomy the next BP reads 72/40.

Which is the best choice?
options: Her heart must be failing: get an urgent echo.
Anaphylaxis: give adrenaline.

Mostly drugs: propofol and too much sevoflurane for her age, on top of losartan and amlodipine, plus lithotomy and fasting. But check the rarer causes: anaphylaxis (skin, wheeze) and arrhythmia (ECG).
questions.explain:
Good. Think drugs, volume, position and surgery, and then deliberately rule out the dangerous rarer causes.

The other choices:
• “Her heart must be failing: get an urgent echo.” Nothing points to heart failure, and she responded to a vasopressor. Start with the common causes.
• “Anaphylaxis: give adrenaline.” Possible in theory, so look for it, but there is no rash or wheeze and a clear drug explanation. Adrenaline for the wrong reason is risky in a 78-year-old.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after induction (hypotension-induction), step 4

questions.stem:
Ten minutes into the resection the BP drifts down again to 80/46, heart rate 62. Your consultant asks for your plan.

The case so far: A 78-year-old woman, 55 kg, for a cystoscopy and resection of a bladder tumour under GA with a supraglottic airway. She takes amlodipine and losartan and took both this morning. Before induction her BP was 165/85. Because of her age your consultant asked you to draw up phenylephrine and ephedrine. Your consultant induced with fentanyl 50 mcg and propofol 70 mg, the airway went in easily, and she is breathing sevoflurane at 2.5%. Your consultant has stepped next door to help a colleague (“Call me if anything changes”). As she is put into lithotomy the next BP reads 72/40.

Which is the best choice?
options: Give 2 L of fluid quickly.
Turn the sevoflurane off: no anaesthetic, no low blood pressure.
Keep the sevoflurane near 1 MAC for her age, repeat ephedrine or phenylephrine boluses, give a modest fluid bolus (250 mL), and if boluses keep being needed, ask about an infusion.
questions.explain:
A sensible plan: enough anaesthetic, small vasopressor doses, a little fluid, and an infusion (phenylephrine or noradrenaline) if she keeps needing boluses, which your consultant decides.

The other choices:
• “Give 2 L of fluid quickly.” Large volumes risk fluid overload in an elderly heart, and the low BP comes from widened vessels, not big losses.
• “Turn the sevoflurane off: no anaesthetic, no low blood pressure.” Awareness under GA is a real harm. Keep enough anaesthetic and support the circulation.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after induction (hypotension-induction), step 5

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old man, 80 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Induction with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium was smooth and he is intubated. Your consultant is beside you writing the chart. You gave cefazolin 2 g IV slowly. Three minutes later the monitor alarms. His face and chest are bright red, and the peak airway pressure has risen from 18 to 32 cmH2O.

What do you do first?
options: Give salbutamol for bronchospasm.
Say it out loud: “I think this is anaphylaxis.” 100% oxygen, stop the antibiotic and anything else running in, and call for more help.
Give phenylephrine 100 mcg for the low BP and watch.
questions.explain:
Flushing, a low BP, a fast heart rate and rising airway pressure minutes after an antibiotic: anaphylaxis until proven otherwise. Naming it gets everyone working on the same problem.

The other choices:
• “Give salbutamol for bronchospasm.” The airways are only part of it: the blood pressure is the immediate threat. Adrenaline treats both.
• “Give phenylephrine 100 mcg for the low BP and watch.” This is not the usual post-induction dip: the flushing, fast heart rate, high airway pressure and timing all point to anaphylaxis. Phenylephrine doesn’t stop the reaction; adrenaline does.
questions.source: MO guide case: Anaphylaxis after the antibiotic (anaphylaxis-antibiotic), step 1

questions.stem:
Help is coming and your consultant agrees. What do you give first?

The case so far: A 40-year-old man, 80 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Induction with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium was smooth and he is intubated. Your consultant is beside you writing the chart. You gave cefazolin 2 g IV slowly. Three minutes later the monitor alarms. His face and chest are bright red, and the peak airway pressure has risen from 18 to 32 cmH2O.
options: Adrenaline 50 mcg IV (0.5 mL of 1:10,000), repeated every 1–2 minutes as needed.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV and an antihistamine first.
Adrenaline 1 mg IV.
Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM into the thigh.
questions.explain:
IV adrenaline in 50 mcg steps is the treatment in theatre, where there is IV access and full monitoring.

The other choices:
• “Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV and an antihistamine first.” These are not first-line: they don’t raise the BP or open the airways in time. Adrenaline first.
• “Adrenaline 1 mg IV.” That is the cardiac arrest dose. In a patient with a pulse it can cause severe hypertension, dangerous arrhythmias and heart damage. Your consultant stops you: 50 mcg IV.
• “Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM into the thigh.” The right drug at the right IM dose, and the choice when there is no IV. In theatre, with a drip and monitoring, small IV doses act faster and are easier to control.
questions.source: MO guide case: Anaphylaxis after the antibiotic (anaphylaxis-antibiotic), step 2

questions.stem:
After two doses of adrenaline 50 mcg the BP is 84/48 and the heart rate 118. He is still wheezy, with a peak pressure of 30 cmH2O.

The case so far: A 40-year-old man, 80 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Induction with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium was smooth and he is intubated. Your consultant is beside you writing the chart. You gave cefazolin 2 g IV slowly. Three minutes later the monitor alarms. His face and chest are bright red, and the peak airway pressure has risen from 18 to 32 cmH2O.

Which is the best choice?
options: Switch to phenylephrine to avoid a fast heart rate.
Stop the adrenaline now the BP is better.

Keep giving adrenaline as needed (your consultant may start an infusion), lie him flat with his legs raised, run in crystalloid fast (20 mL/kg, about 1.6 L for him, repeated as needed) and give salbutamol for the wheeze.
questions.explain:
Anaphylaxis leaks a lot of fluid out of the vessels: adults often need litres. Keep the adrenaline going until he is stable, and treat the bronchospasm.

The other choices:
• “Switch to phenylephrine to avoid a fast heart rate.” Adrenaline is the treatment: it supports the heart, opens the airways and calms the reaction. Phenylephrine does only one of those.
• “Stop the adrenaline now the BP is better.” Anaphylaxis often rebounds. Keep treating until the BP is stable; many patients need several doses or an infusion.
questions.source: MO guide case: Anaphylaxis after the antibiotic (anaphylaxis-antibiotic), step 3

questions.stem:
Fifteen minutes later he is stable: BP 108/64, heart rate 102, the wheeze gone. Surgery has not started. Your consultant asks: “What now?”

The case so far: A 40-year-old man, 80 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Induction with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium was smooth and he is intubated. Your consultant is beside you writing the chart. You gave cefazolin 2 g IV slowly. Three minutes later the monitor alarms. His face and chest are bright red, and the peak airway pressure has risen from 18 to 32 cmH2O.

Which is the best choice?
options: Carry on with the surgery now he is stable.
Take blood for mast cell tryptase now, and plan repeat samples at 1–2 hours and after 24 hours. With the surgeon, postpone the operation (your consultant decides) and plan where he goes next.
Tryptase can wait for tomorrow’s blood tests.
questions.explain:
Tryptase confirms anaphylaxis afterwards. Take the first sample once he is stable enough, without delaying treatment, then repeat. Postponing a non-urgent operation is usual.

The other choices:
• “Carry on with the surgery now he is stable.” He may rebound, and the operation isn’t urgent. Postponing is usual; your consultant and the surgeon decide.
• “Tryptase can wait for tomorrow’s blood tests.” Tryptase peaks within 1–2 hours and then falls. Take the first sample as soon as he is stable, then repeat.
questions.source: MO guide case: Anaphylaxis after the antibiotic (anaphylaxis-antibiotic), step 4

questions.stem:
Before he leaves theatre, your consultant asks you to help with the follow-up.

The case so far: A 40-year-old man, 80 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Induction with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium was smooth and he is intubated. Your consultant is beside you writing the chart. You gave cefazolin 2 g IV slowly. Three minutes later the monitor alarms. His face and chest are bright red, and the peak airway pressure has risen from 18 to 32 cmH2O.

Which is the best choice?
options: Record every drug and the time it was given, explain to him what happened once he is awake, make sure your consultant’s allergy clinic referral is done, and record a suspected reaction to all the drugs he had until testing finds the cause.
Record “allergic to cefazolin” and nothing else.
Don’t tell him: it would only worry him.
questions.explain:
Any of the drugs (cefazolin, rocuronium, propofol, fentanyl, or chlorhexidine on the skin) could be the cause. Only allergy testing can say which, so list them all, and report it as an adverse drug reaction.

The other choices:
• “Record “allergic to cefazolin” and nothing else.” Cefazolin is the likeliest culprit, but muscle relaxants and chlorhexidine are common causes too. Labelling one drug without testing can miss the real cause.
• “Don’t tell him: it would only worry him.” He needs to know, for his safety at every future operation, and he has a right to know. Tell him clearly once he is awake.
questions.source: MO guide case: Anaphylaxis after the antibiotic (anaphylaxis-antibiotic), step 5

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman, 60 kg, who smokes, has had a knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway (LMA). At the end your consultant is with you: “Take the LMA out when she’s ready.” She starts coughing and moving her arms, so you take it out. Thirty seconds later she makes a high-pitched crowing noise, then silence. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw, the reservoir bag doesn’t move and the capnograph is flat.

What do you do first?
options: Suction her mouth and wait for it to settle.
Put the LMA back in.
Squeeze the bag as hard as you can with the APL valve closed.
Call out “Laryngospasm”. 100% oxygen with a tight two-hand mask seal, a firm jaw thrust, and close the APL valve partly to give continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
questions.explain:
Exactly the first steps. A firm jaw thrust (pressing just behind the angle of the jaw) and steady CPAP often open the cords on their own.

The other choices:
• “Suction her mouth and wait for it to settle.” Gentle suction of the mouth is fine, but waiting while she can’t breathe lets the saturation fall fast. Act now.
• “Put the LMA back in.” The cords are shut below the LMA: putting it back doesn’t open them, and fiddling in the mouth of a lightly anaesthetised patient makes the spasm worse.
• “Squeeze the bag as hard as you can with the APL valve closed.” Hard squeezes against closed cords blow gas into the stomach. Steady CPAP with a good seal is gentler and works better.
questions.source: MO guide case: Laryngospasm after the LMA comes out (laryngospasm-emergence), step 1

questions.stem:
With CPAP and a jaw thrust a little gas moves with a high-pitched noise, but the saturation keeps falling. Your consultant is at your side.

The case so far: A 24-year-old woman, 60 kg, who smokes, has had a knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway (LMA). At the end your consultant is with you: “Take the LMA out when she’s ready.” She starts coughing and moving her arms, so you take it out. Thirty seconds later she makes a high-pitched crowing noise, then silence. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw, the reservoir bag doesn’t move and the capnograph is flat.

Which is the best choice?
options: Keep going with CPAP alone for another minute.
Deepen her with propofol 30 mg IV (about 0.5 mg/kg), keeping the CPAP on.
Give suxamethonium straight away.
questions.explain:
A small dose of propofol deepens the anaesthetic and often relaxes the cords. Keep the CPAP and jaw thrust going.

The other choices:
• “Keep going with CPAP alone for another minute.” CPAP is worth a short try, but she is desaturating. Move to the next step: deepen her.
• “Give suxamethonium straight away.” Reasonable if she is desaturating fast, and your consultant may choose it. Many give propofol first because it often works, but suxamethonium is the definitive treatment.
questions.source: MO guide case: Laryngospasm after the LMA comes out (laryngospasm-emergence), step 2

questions.stem:
After the propofol the noise changes, but very little gas moves. SpO2 82%, heart rate 98.

The case so far: A 24-year-old woman, 60 kg, who smokes, has had a knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway (LMA). At the end your consultant is with you: “Take the LMA out when she’s ready.” She starts coughing and moving her arms, so you take it out. Thirty seconds later she makes a high-pitched crowing noise, then silence. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw, the reservoir bag doesn’t move and the capnograph is flat.

Which is the best choice?
options: Get ready for front of neck access.
Another 30 mg of propofol.
Suxamethonium 30 mg IV (about 0.5 mg/kg) as your consultant asks, keep the CPAP on, and have atropine ready for a slow heart.
questions.explain:
A small dose of suxamethonium relaxes the cords within a minute; a full intubating dose (1–1.5 mg/kg) is used if she needs a tube. Suxamethonium can slow the heart, especially in a hypoxic patient, so have atropine ready.

The other choices:
• “Get ready for front of neck access.” Too early. Laryngospasm almost always breaks with suxamethonium. Front of neck access is for “can’t intubate, can’t oxygenate” after everything else has failed.
• “Another 30 mg of propofol.” She is now hypoxic, and more propofol lowers the BP without reliably opening the cords. It is time for the relaxant.
questions.source: MO guide case: Laryngospasm after the LMA comes out (laryngospasm-emergence), step 3

questions.stem:
Within a minute the bag moves easily, the capnograph trace returns and SpO2 climbs to 97%. She isn’t breathing yet because of the suxamethonium.

The case so far: A 24-year-old woman, 60 kg, who smokes, has had a knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway (LMA). At the end your consultant is with you: “Take the LMA out when she’s ready.” She starts coughing and moving her arms, so you take it out. Thirty seconds later she makes a high-pitched crowing noise, then silence. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw, the reservoir bag doesn’t move and the capnograph is flat.

Which is the best choice?
options: Take the mask off and see whether she breathes.
Keep bagging with 100% oxygen until she breathes again (5–10 minutes), keep her asleep so she isn’t awake while paralysed, and listen to her chest for crackles.
Let her wake up now: the spasm is over.
questions.explain:
Right. She must stay asleep until the suxamethonium wears off. Crackles or pink froth would suggest fluid in the lungs from breathing hard against closed cords.

The other choices:
• “Take the mask off and see whether she breathes.” She can’t breathe yet: she is paralysed. Keep ventilating with the mask.
• “Let her wake up now: the spasm is over.” She is paralysed. Waking now means being awake and unable to move or breathe: awareness. Keep her asleep and ventilated until the suxamethonium wears off.
questions.source: MO guide case: Laryngospasm after the LMA comes out (laryngospasm-emergence), step 4

questions.stem:
Her breathing returns, strong and regular. Your consultant lets her wake fully with the mask on; she opens her eyes and obeys commands. What do you do before PACU?

The case so far: A 24-year-old woman, 60 kg, who smokes, has had a knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway (LMA). At the end your consultant is with you: “Take the LMA out when she’s ready.” She starts coughing and moving her arms, so you take it out. Thirty seconds later she makes a high-pitched crowing noise, then silence. Her chest and abdomen move in a see-saw, the reservoir bag doesn’t move and the capnograph is flat.
options: Hand over the laryngospasm to the PACU team: watch for pink frothy sputum and falling saturation over the next few hours. Warn her about muscle aches from suxamethonium, and record it all.
Tell the PACU nurse, but leave it out of the notes so it doesn’t alarm her.
She looks fine, so there’s no need to mention it.
questions.explain:
Negative pressure pulmonary oedema can appear up to a few hours later. The PACU nurse needs to know what to look for.

The other choices:
• “Tell the PACU nurse, but leave it out of the notes so it doesn’t alarm her.” It belongs in the notes, and she should hear about it from you: it may matter at her next anaesthetic.
• “She looks fine, so there’s no need to mention it.” The PACU team needs to know, because problems can appear later, and so does she, for next time. Hand it over and write it down.
questions.source: MO guide case: Laryngospasm after the LMA comes out (laryngospasm-emergence), step 5

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old woman, 65 kg, arrived in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) 15 minutes ago after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA. The PACU nurse calls you: “Pain score 8 out of 10, and she feels sick.” She is curled up, retching and holding her right shoulder.

What do you do first?
options: Give ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea.
Phone the primary anaesthetist.
Go now. Check airway, breathing and circulation and the vitals, then read the anaesthetic chart (what she was given, when, and any allergies) before giving anything.
Give morphine 5 mg IV straight away: she is clearly in pain.
questions.explain:
The handbook rule for PACU: see the patient, then check the anaesthetic chart before giving any drug. It prevents double doses and drug errors.

The other choices:
• “Give ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea.” Check the chart first: she had ondansetron at the end of surgery. Another dose of the same drug within 6 hours adds little.
• “Phone the primary anaesthetist.” Not wrong, but pain and nausea are the PACU MO’s job; the primary anaesthetist hears about problems that persist or are severe. See her and read the chart first.
• “Give morphine 5 mg IV straight away: she is clearly in pain.” The nurse stops you: “She had morphine 5 mg 40 minutes ago.” The handbook rule: check the anaesthetic chart before giving any drug in PACU.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: pain and nausea (pacu-pain-ponv), step 1

questions.stem:
The chart: fentanyl 100 mcg at induction; morphine 5 mg 40 minutes ago; paracetamol 1 g and parecoxib 40 mg IV; dexamethasone 8 mg at induction; ondansetron 4 mg at the end; local anaesthetic at the port sites. No allergies. She is alert, breathing 20 a minute. The pain is in her right shoulder and around the wounds.

The case so far: A 45-year-old woman, 65 kg, arrived in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) 15 minutes ago after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA. The PACU nurse calls you: “Pain score 8 out of 10, and she feels sick.” She is curled up, retching and holding her right shoulder.

Which is the best choice?
options: Morphine 1–2 mg IV every 5–10 minutes, checking pain, sedation and breathing between doses; stop if she becomes drowsy or her breathing rate falls below 10. If she still hurts after about 0.1 mg/kg (about 6 mg for her) in PACU, call the primary anaesthetist.
Morphine 10 mg IV now to get on top of it.
Tramadol 100 mg IV.
Paracetamol 1 g IV.
questions.explain:
Small doses with a check between each, so you find the dose she needs without overshooting. Morphine peaks 15–20 minutes after each dose, so doses stack up if you go too fast, especially in the elderly, in kidney impairment and in sleep apnoea.

The other choices:
• “Morphine 10 mg IV now to get on top of it.” A large single dose on top of the morphine she already had risks oversedation and slowed breathing. Titrate in small steps.
• “Tramadol 100 mg IV.” Tramadol is too weak for this level of pain and is itself a common cause of nausea and vomiting.
• “Paracetamol 1 g IV.” She had paracetamol 1 g in theatre; the next dose isn’t due for 6 hours. Try again.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: pain and nausea (pacu-pain-ponv), step 2

questions.stem:
Twenty minutes on she is awake and breathing well. Her pain is 4/10, mostly shoulder-tip pain from the gas under her diaphragm. But she still feels sick and has vomited once.

The case so far: A 45-year-old woman, 65 kg, arrived in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) 15 minutes ago after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA. The PACU nurse calls you: “Pain score 8 out of 10, and she feels sick.” She is curled up, retching and holding her right shoulder.

Which is the best choice?
options: Check for causes other than drugs (low BP, low oxygen, pain), then give metoclopramide 10 mg IV slowly: a different class from what she has had.
Ondansetron 4 mg again.
Dexamethasone 8 mg again.
Haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV.
questions.explain:
Rescue with a drug from a class she hasn’t had: she had dexamethasone and ondansetron, so metoclopramide (a dopamine blocker) is a good choice. Avoid it in Parkinson’s disease and bowel obstruction.

The other choices:
• “Ondansetron 4 mg again.” She had ondansetron less than an hour ago. Repeating the same class within 6 hours adds little. Choose a different class.
• “Dexamethasone 8 mg again.” Dexamethasone works slowly and is for prevention; she had it at induction.
• “Haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV.” A reasonable rescue from another class, but it lengthens the QT interval (so does the ondansetron she has had): check the ECG first, and never give it in Parkinson’s disease. Metoclopramide is the usual first choice here.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: pain and nausea (pacu-pain-ponv), step 3

questions.stem:
Thirty minutes later she is comfortable (pain 3/10), no longer nauseated, and keen to go back to the ward.

The case so far: A 45-year-old woman, 65 kg, arrived in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) 15 minutes ago after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA. The PACU nurse calls you: “Pain score 8 out of 10, and she feels sick.” She is curled up, retching and holding her right shoulder.

Which is the best choice?
options: Send her now: she is comfortable.

Record each drug you gave with the dose and time, make sure she has been watched long enough after her last IV morphine, and write a ward plan: regular paracetamol, an NSAID if suitable, an oral opioid if needed, and antiemetics from different classes if needed.
No need to write anything: the nurse records the drugs.
questions.explain:
A clear record and a plan stop the ward repeating doses or leaving her in pain. IV morphine has its biggest effect on breathing about 15–20 minutes after a dose, so watch her past that.

The other choices:
• “Send her now: she is comfortable.” Make sure enough time has passed since her last IV morphine to see its full effect on breathing (about 15–20 minutes), that she has had the minimum 30 minutes in PACU, and that what you gave is recorded.
• “No need to write anything: the nurse records the drugs.” Drugs you give are your responsibility to record, with the dose and time. The ward also needs a plan.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: pain and nausea (pacu-pain-ponv), step 4

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old man, 68 kg, with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), arrived in PACU 30 minutes ago after an open inguinal hernia repair under GA. The PACU nurse calls you urgently: “He’s very drowsy, breathing 7 a minute, sats 88 on 2 litres.”

What do you do first?
options: Read his anaesthetic chart at the desk first.
Tell the nurse to give naloxone 400 mcg IV now, and come when you can.

Go now. Call his name loudly and shake his shoulder, jaw thrust if he is obstructing, face-mask oxygen at 15 L/min, and tell him to take deep breaths. Ask the nurse to get naloxone and call the primary anaesthetist.
questions.explain:
The handbook: when a PACU nurse alerts you, go at once and check airway, breathing and circulation. Stimulation alone often gets an opioid-sedated patient breathing again.

The other choices:
• “Read his anaesthetic chart at the desk first.” The chart matters before you give a drug, but airway and breathing come first. Go to the bedside now.
• “Tell the nurse to give naloxone 400 mcg IV now, and come when you can.” You need to see him, and 400 mcg at once reverses all of his pain relief as well as the sedation.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 1

questions.stem:
With stimulation and oxygen he opens his eyes to a loud voice and breathes 9 a minute while you talk to him, but drifts off and slows to 6 when you stop. His pupils are pinpoint. The nurse hands you the chart: fentanyl 100 mcg at induction; morphine 10 mg during surgery; rocuronium 50 mg at induction and 10 mg an hour later, reversed with neostigmine 2.5 mg and glycopyrrolate 0.4 mg; no train-of-four recorded. No benzodiazepines.

The case so far: A 72-year-old man, 68 kg, with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), arrived in PACU 30 minutes ago after an open inguinal hernia repair under GA. The PACU nurse calls you urgently: “He’s very drowsy, breathing 7 a minute, sats 88 on 2 litres.”

Which is the best choice?
options: This looks like too much opioid for him: morphine’s active breakdown products build up when the kidneys are poor. Give naloxone in small steps.
Give flumazenil.
Keep stimulating him: it will wear off.
questions.explain:
Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, morphine 10 mg in a 72-year-old with poor kidneys: opioid excess is the likely cause.

The other choices:
• “Give flumazenil.” There is no benzodiazepine on the chart. Flumazenil won’t help and can cause seizures. Try again.
• “Keep stimulating him: it will wear off.” In kidney disease morphine’s effects can last for hours. As soon as you stop talking, he stops breathing. He needs treatment.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 2

questions.stem:
How much naloxone do you give?

The case so far: A 72-year-old man, 68 kg, with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), arrived in PACU 30 minutes ago after an open inguinal hernia repair under GA. The PACU nurse calls you urgently: “He’s very drowsy, breathing 7 a minute, sats 88 on 2 litres.”
options: Naloxone 400 mcg IV in one go.
Naloxone 40 mcg IV (dilute 400 mcg to 10 mL and give 1 mL), repeated every 2 minutes until he breathes over 10 a minute and is rousable.
Wait for the primary anaesthetist before giving naloxone.
questions.explain:
Small steps restore breathing without stripping away all his pain relief. The aim is breathing, not wide awake.

The other choices:
• “Naloxone 400 mcg IV in one go.” A full dose at once reverses everything: sudden severe pain, high BP, a fast heart and, rarely, fluid on the lungs.
• “Wait for the primary anaesthetist before giving naloxone.” Slow breathing with falling saturation can’t wait. Small doses of naloxone are a PACU MO’s job; call the anaesthetist as well, not instead.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 3

questions.stem:
Now he is awake, breathing 12 a minute and talking, pain 3/10. But his breaths are shallow and jerky, he can’t lift his head off the pillow for 5 seconds, and his grip is weak.

The case so far: A 72-year-old man, 68 kg, with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), arrived in PACU 30 minutes ago after an open inguinal hernia repair under GA. The PACU nurse calls you urgently: “He’s very drowsy, breathing 7 a minute, sats 88 on 2 litres.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Suspect muscle relaxant still working: check the train-of-four (TOF) with a nerve stimulator and tell the primary anaesthetist. Further reversal is their decision.
More naloxone.
Another dose of neostigmine 2.5 mg.
questions.explain:
Shallow, jerky breathing, a weak head lift and a weak grip after a top-up of rocuronium with no TOF recorded: residual block until proven otherwise. Neostigmine works reliably only once the TOF count is 4; given at a lower count, or without checking, it can leave the patient weak.

The other choices:
• “More naloxone.” The opioid effect is already reversed: he is awake and breathing faster. Weakness with shallow breathing points to muscle relaxant still working.
• “Another dose of neostigmine 2.5 mg.” Neostigmine has a ceiling: beyond about 0.05 mg/kg (5 mg at most) it adds side effects, not strength. Further reversal is the primary anaesthetist’s decision.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 4

questions.stem:
The TOF ratio is 0.6; it needs to be over 0.9. The primary anaesthetist arrives and gives sugammadex 2 mg/kg (about 140 mg). Within 2 minutes he lifts his head, grips strongly and breathes deeply. The nurse asks whether he can go to the ward.

The case so far: A 72-year-old man, 68 kg, with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), arrived in PACU 30 minutes ago after an open inguinal hernia repair under GA. The PACU nurse calls you urgently: “He’s very drowsy, breathing 7 a minute, sats 88 on 2 litres.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Not yet. Naloxone wears off in 30–60 minutes, before morphine does. Keep him monitored for at least 2 hours after the last naloxone dose (longer is safer with morphine and poor kidneys), ask the primary anaesthetist whether he needs a monitored bed (their decision), avoid more morphine, and record everything.
Send him to the ward with a dose of naloxone written up in case.
Yes: he is awake and strong now.
questions.explain:
The danger is the naloxone wearing off while the morphine is still working. Watch him long enough, and leave the monitored-bed decision to a senior.

The other choices:
• “Send him to the ward with a dose of naloxone written up in case.” A dose written up only helps if someone notices in time. He needs watching where staff can see him, for at least 2 hours after his last naloxone.
• “Yes: he is awake and strong now.” Naloxone lasts less than an hour; in kidney disease morphine’s effects last much longer.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 5

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement.
